units.text: Start with the shared private hosted zone at the top. Its records can serve associated VPCs across Regions; this does not make Resolver endpoints global.
Compare the two regional panels. Each Region needs its own appropriate Resolver endpoints, rules and hybrid connectivity, with resilient endpoint addresses across Availability Zones.
Read the corporate forwarder boxes and bottom guidance. Choose deliberate regional targets and test failures instead of assuming endpoint configuration replicates automatically.
With the complete slide visible, distinguish DNS availability from application reachability and data readiness. A successful cross-region answer does not create the application's network path.
Trace the signing panel on the left. Route fifty-three signs public hosted-zone records; the parent DS record connects the zone's key to the DNSSEC chain of trust.
Move to the validation panel. The VPC Resolver checks signed public responses during recursive resolution. Invalid signatures or a broken required trust chain can cause SERVFAIL.
Read the lower cards. Signing and validation protect authenticity and integrity, not confidentiality. Monitor keys and signing health, and plan rollover and rollback carefully.
Return to the full slide. Public zone signing and VPC validation are separate settings. An unsigned delegation is not automatically invalid, and DNSSEC does not replace transport encryption.

Compare timeout and name-not-found on the left. No timely answer calls for resolver reachability checks; NXDOMAIN calls for examining the exact name, selected zone, forwarding rules and cached results.
Now compare NODATA and SERVFAIL on the right. Check the requested record type and policy responses for NODATA. Investigate upstream failures, validation and loops when resolution cannot complete.
Follow the evidence sequence below. Record the caller, exact query, responding resolver and status, effective zone or rule, and relevant logs or cache before changing configuration.

With the original slide visible, reproduce using the same client, resolver and record type. A valid DNS answer followed by an application failure moves the investigation to connectivity, TLS or the application.
Begin with the corporate network and namespace boxes. Corporate DNS owns the corporate suffix; AWS private zones hold the AWS suffix. Forward each namespace toward its intended authority.
Move to the central DNS account and workload accounts. Share the right configuration and associate it with authorized VPCs, retaining clear ownership of zones, Profiles and forwarding rules.

Inspect both Regions and the operational cards. Use endpoint interface addresses across Availability Zones, private routes and approved DNS access. Monitor query behavior and exercise failure scenarios.

Review the full scenario. Test both query directions from actual clients, account for cached answers, and keep application reachability separate. Estimate endpoint, query and logging costs for the chosen design.
